extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and examiners (patent attorneys/agents, inventors, USPTO examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and evaluating a U.S. patent specification to satisfy the three separate requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph: written description, enablement (manner and process of making and using), and best mode. Used by patent prosecutors and examiners when drafting claims/specifications or determining compliance with §112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention (35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph). The written description requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must show that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention. Case law (e.g., Ariad Pharm., Inc. v. Eli Lilly; Vas‑Cath v. Mahurkar; In re Barker; Vasudevan Software v. MicroStrategy) reiterates that written description and enablement are distinct inquiries. Examples: lack of literal recitation of a claim term (e.g., 'disparate databases') in the specification does not necessarily preclude a genuine issue of material fact as to possession if the specification contains some discussion supporting the claim. See MPEP §2161 and related MPEP sections (2163, 2165).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (Manner and Process of Making and Using)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall describe the manner and process of making and using the invention in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention (the enablement requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a distinct statutory requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The inquiry asks whether a person skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention based on the disclosure. The MPEP emphasizes that a disclosure can be enabling without necessarily describing the invention in the written‑description sense. Examples: a specification might disclose methods enabling certain formulations (broadly defined functional ingredients) but not describe any specific formulation in a way that satisfies written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention (statutory best mode requirement in 35 U.S.C. 112(a) / pre‑AIA first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode is a separate and distinct requirement from both written description and enablement. The specification must disclose the best mode the inventor contemplated for practicing the invention so that a person skilled in the art can carry it out. See MPEP §2165 and considerations in MPEP 2165.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Must Describe the Invention Completely (Full, Clear, Concise, Exact Terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must provide a complete description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it in such 'full, clear, concise, and exact terms' as to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory language from 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and the pre‑AIA first paragraph and underlies both the written description and enablement inquiries. Practitioners should ensure the specification contains sufficient detail across embodiments to permit practice of the invention and to support the claimed scope. MPEP repeatedly cites this statutory standard when explaining the three separate requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope Commensurate with Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim scope must be commensurate with the disclosure; the written description must support the breadth of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP and cited cases make clear that claims cannot properly be given a scope broader than what the specification demonstrates the inventor possessed. Examiners and practitioners should evaluate whether the specification provides support for the breadth of claims (possession of claimed subject matter). The page cites examples (e.g., functional vs. specific disclosures, software examples) and refers to MPEP sections on 'possession of the invention' and 'scope commensurate with disclosure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Distinctions: Description Without Enablement and Enablement Without Description
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be described without the disclosure being enabling, and conversely a disclosure could be enabling without describing the invention in the written‑description sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: a chemical compound might be described (written description) but lack a disclosed or apparent method of making it (so not enabled); a specification describing methods of making and using a paint composition with functionally defined ingredients over broad ranges might enable formulations but not describe any specific formulation for written‑description purposes. See In re Armbruster and related case law. Use these distinctions when analyzing §112 compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the Three §112 Requirements as Separate and Distinct Inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description, enablement, and best mode are separate and distinct requirements and should be considered individually when evaluating a specification under §112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP cites Ariad and other authorities to stress that if Congress had intended enablement to be the sole description requirement the statute would have been written differently. Examiners and counsel must evaluate each requirement on its own facts and record; failures in one area do not automatically prove failures in another. The MPEP repeats this admonition in multiple subsections.
